In [[mathematics]], the '''Drinfeld upper half plane''' is a [[rigid analytic space]] analogous to the usual [[upper half plane]] for function fields, introduced by {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Vladimir Drinfeld|last=Drinfeld|year=1976}}. 
It is defined to be the set difference '''P'''<sup>1</sup>('''C''') \ '''P'''<sup>1</sup>('''F'''<sub>∞</sub>), where '''F''' is a function field of a curve over a [[finite field]], '''F'''<sub>∞</sub> its completion at ∞, and '''C''' the completion of the [[algebraic closure]] of '''F'''<sub>∞</sub>.

The analogy with the usual upper half plane arises from the fact that the [[global function field]] '''F''' is analogous to the rational numbers '''Q'''. Then, '''F'''<sub>∞</sub> is the real numbers '''R''' and the algebraic closure of '''F'''<sub>∞</sub> is the complex numbers '''C''' (which are already complete). Finally, '''P'''<sup>1</sup>('''C''') is the [[Riemann sphere]], so '''P'''<sup>1</sup>('''C''') \ '''P'''<sup>1</sup>('''R''') is the upper half plane ''together with'' the lower half plane.
